extracted.intended_audience: employers, workplace safety managers, safety coordinators, and occupational health professionals responsible for complying with OSHA heat-related protections
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and proposed regulatory requirements for developing and implementing a Heat Injury and Illness Prevention Plan (HIIPP), defining heat-related terms, and monitoring/identifying heat hazards at work sites to trigger protective measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indoors / indoor (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Means an area enclosed within a structure by perimeter walls, doors, windows, dividers, or other physical barriers that restrict airflow, whether open or closed; construction activity is considered indoor when performed inside a structure after the outside walls and roof are erected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides examples (garage, interior of a warehouse, shed) and explains why the term is defined (used in definitions for outdoor/outdoors and several proposed paragraphs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial heat trigger (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Means a heat index of 80 °F or a WBGT equal to the NIOSH Recommended Alert Limit (RAL).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that exposures at/above the initial trigger require implementation of controls (drinking water, break area(s), indoor work area controls, acclimatization, rest breaks if needed, effective communication, PPE cooling property maintenance). Scientific basis explained in Section V.B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outdoor / outdoors (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Means an area that is not indoors; vehicles operated outdoors are considered outdoor work areas unless exempted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives examples (agricultural fields, under canopies and pavilions) and notes where this definition is used in proposed paragraphs (d), (e), and (h).

rubrics_metrics.name: Radiant heat (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Means heat transferred by electromagnetic waves between surfaces; sources include the sun, hot objects, hot liquids, hot surfaces, and fire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes radiant heat can transfer across distances without contact; infrared radiation common in foundries and metal/glass industries. Defined because it is included in WBGT definition and used in paragraph (e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended Alert Limit (RAL) (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Means the NIOSH-recommended heat stress alert limits for unacclimatized workers; the initial heat trigger incorporates the NIOSH RAL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes NIOSH RAL purpose, environmental/ metabolic considerations, assumption of conventional one-layer work clothing, and presents formula: RAL [°C−WBGT] = 59.9 - 14.1 log10 M[W].

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended Exposure Limit (REL) (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Means the NIOSH-recommended heat stress exposure limits for acclimatized workers; the high heat trigger incorporates the NIOSH REL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains REL purpose, environmental/metabolic basis, clothing assumption, and gives formula: REL [°C−WBGT] = 56.7 - 11.5 log10 M[W].

rubrics_metrics.name: Shade (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defined as the blockage of direct sunlight such that objects do not cast a shadow in the area of blocked sunlight; shade can be artificial or naturally occurring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included to clarify use of shade as a control in outdoor break areas under proposed paragraph (e)(3)(i).

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs and symptoms of heat-related illness (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Means physiological manifestations of a heat-related illness, including headache, nausea, weakness, dizziness, elevated body temperature, muscle cramps, and muscle pain or spasms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to define scenarios requiring employer procedures to respond to affected employees and to specify training and monitoring requirements (paragraphs (g), (h), (f)(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs and symptoms of a heat emergency (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Means physiological manifestations that require emergency response and include loss of consciousness (fainting, collapse) with excessive body temperature, possibly accompanied by vertigo, nausea, headache, cerebral dysfunction, bizarre behavior, staggering, vomiting, convulsions, or a persistently elevated heart rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defined to clarify when employers must have emergency response procedures and which symptoms require immediate emergency action; used in proposed paragraphs (g) and (h)(iv).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vapor-impermeable clothing (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Means full-body clothing that significantly inhibits or completely prevents sweat produced by the body from evaporating into the outside air (e.g., encapsulating suits, chemical resistant suits); excludes vapor-permeable PPE and small-area vapor-impermeable items unless part of whole-body ensembles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included because employers with employees wearing such clothing would be required to evaluate heat stress hazards and implement policies/procedures based on reputable sources; gives examples and notes manufacturers' product information can be used to determine qualification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vehicle (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Means a car, truck, van, or other motorized means of transporting people or goods; may include forklifts, bulldozers, tractors, cranes, etc.; a vehicle is a work area when a worker's activities occur in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that vehicles can constitute work areas for purposes of the standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wet Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT) (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A heat metric accounting for ambient temperature, humidity, radiant heat, and air movement; separate formulas exist for indoor vs outdoor measurement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by NIOSH and ACGIH for occupational heat stress evaluation; used in definitions for heat triggers and in proposed paragraphs (c) and (d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Work area (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: An area where one or more employees are working within a work site; includes any area where an employee performs any work-related activity and may be on or off employer premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referenced in many proposed provisions including scope, HIIPP, identifying heat hazards, and requirements at/above triggers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work site (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A physical location (fixed or mobile) where the employer's work or operations are performed; includes all areas associated with the employer's operations and any space an employee might occupy arriving, working, or leaving; may or may not be under employer control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defined because it is referenced across the proposed standard (HIIPP, identifying heat hazards, requirements for triggers, training, recordkeeping).

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop and implement a comprehensive HIIPP for each work site (c)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must develop and implement a comprehensive Heat Injury and Illness Prevention Plan for each work site; if multiple work sites are substantially similar, HIIPPs may be developed by work site type provided site-specific information is included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For employer-controlled and non-controlled areas, plan must include procedures ensuring compliance (e.g., communication, hazard alerts). Reference to NIOSH criteria and state standards supports the requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: HIIPP must list types of work activities covered (c)(2)(i)
rubrics_metrics.description: The HIIPP must include a comprehensive list of the types of work activities covered by the plan (e.g., outdoor work at/above initial trigger for at least 15 minutes per 60-minute period).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided (landscaping employees); see scope and application explanations for coverage details.

rubrics_metrics.name: HIIPP must include policies and procedures to comply with standard (c)(2)(ii)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must include the policies and procedures necessary to comply with the requirements of the proposed standard (paragraphs (d) through (j)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: HIIPP must be adaptable to site/job characteristics; employers may include additional policies/procedures to comply with federal/state/local laws. Explanation sections give examples of compliance methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: HIIPP must identify heat metric to be monitored (c)(2)(iii)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must identify in the HIIPP the heat metric (heat index or WBGT) that will be monitored to comply with paragraph (d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to Explanation for heat index and WBGT for considerations when selecting metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate and document hazards from vapor-impermeable clothing (c)(3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where employees wear vapor-impermeable clothing, employers must evaluate heat stress hazards resulting from the clothing and implement policies/procedures based on reputable sources; document the evaluation and include policies in the HIIPP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazard evaluation should include review of environmental exposures, high-risk areas/tasks/occupations, and duration/intensity of tasks while wearing the clothing. Examples of reputable sources: NIOSH (2016), ACGIH (2023). Example policy: apply protections at lower temperature thresholds. Employers should communicate status of actions to affected employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written HIIPP required for employers with >10 employees (c)(4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers with more than 10 employees must develop and implement a written HIIPP; employers with 10 or fewer employees may communicate HIIPP orally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: complexity and multiple locations/shifts increase miscommunication risk; small employers may still opt to write plans. Existing plans must be evaluated and updated to meet requirements; training required for modifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designate heat safety coordinator(s) with authority and training (c)(5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must designate one or more workplace heat safety coordinators to implement and monitor the HIIPP; any trained employee capable of the role may be designated; for employers with >10 employees, identity must be documented in the written HIIPP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinator(s) must receive training required by proposed paragraphs (h)(1) and (2) and have authority to ensure compliance; possible duties include site inspections and monitoring employee behaviors (drinking water, rest breaks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicit input from non-managerial employees and representatives (c)(6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must seek input and involvement of non-managerial employees and their representatives in developing and implementing the HIIPP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods include safety meetings, safety committees, supervisor conversations, negotiated processes, anonymous suggestion boxes; method may vary by employer size. Employers should consider union safety committees where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review/evaluate HIIPP after serious heat-related events and at least annually (c)(7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must review and evaluate the effectiveness of the HIIPP whenever a heat-related injury/illness occurs resulting in death, days away from work, medical treatment beyond first aid, or loss of consciousness, and at least annually; update the HIIPP as necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers must seek employee input during reviews/updates; update-triggered retraining requirements are specified under paragraph (h). OSHA expects immediate correction of identified deficiencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make HIIPP readily available at the work site during each shift (c)(8)
rubrics_metrics.description: The employer must make the HIIPP readily accessible to all employees performing work at the work site during each shift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper copies, electronic access (smartphone) and other alternatives permitted provided no barriers to immediate access are created.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure HIIPP is available in a language employees understand (c)(9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must ensure the HIIPP is available in a language each employee, supervisor, and heat safety coordinator understands; for employers with >10 employees, written translations are required in all languages employees understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers may use translator programs if they can ensure translation accuracy. If employees are illiterate, employers must ensure someone is available to read/explain the plan. For employers with ≤10 employees, an available person to explain the plan suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor outdoor heat conditions using forecasts or on-site measurements (d)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers with outdoor work sites must monitor heat conditions at outdoor work areas by either tracking local heat index forecasts from reputable sources or making on-site measurements using monitoring device(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reputable forecast sources include local NWS office, OSHA-NIOSH Heat Safety Tool, or other weather apps; when using forecasts, employers must accurately enter work area location (beware GPS auto-location).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult forecasts or monitoring devices frequently enough to detect initial/high triggers (d)(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must consult the chosen forecast or monitoring device(s) frequently enough to determine with reasonable accuracy when conditions reach the initial or high heat triggers; forecasts should be checked as close to the start of the work shift as possible and short-term (hourly) forecasts used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employer responsible for ensuring required controls are in place when triggers are met; frequency of monitoring should be decided with that responsibility in mind. Example: if forecast indicates triggers for last 4 hours, employer may implement controls for those hours or consult again later to refine timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-site monitoring device placement and multi-area application (d)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: On-site monitoring devices should be set up at or as close as possible to the work area (e.g., on a tripod a few yards away); a single device may be used for multiple work areas if there's no reasonable anticipation of differing heat exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If exposures may differ between areas, measure the area with the highest expected exposure and apply that value to all employees rather than measuring each area; example given for harvesting in different fields within a mile under similar conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Device calibration and following manufacturer's manual (d)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers conducting on-site monitoring should consult user manuals and ensure devices are calibrated and in working order, following the device manufacturer's manual when conducting monitoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures measurement accuracy and appropriate use of monitoring equipment.

rubrics_metrics.name: WBGT-specific measurement considerations (d)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers using WBGT must take into account differences in solar radiation and wind when deciding whether a single measurement can be used for multiple work areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measurements in shaded areas should not be applied to non-shaded areas; solar exposure and wind materially affect WBGT readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat index monitoring options (d)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers using heat index may use heat index monitors or measure temperature and humidity separately and calculate heat index (e.g., using NWS heat index calculator).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If measuring temp and humidity separately, employers need to use a heat index calculator to derive the monitored metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop a reasonable measurement strategy adapted to expected conditions (d)(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers who conduct on-site monitoring must develop a measurement strategy appropriate to expected conditions; if forecasts show no approach to initial trigger, measurements may not be needed, but where temperatures may approach triggers several timely measurements may be necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measurement frequency should increase as the hottest part of the day approaches. Employers should balance forecast and on-site data to determine monitoring cadence.
